title: Free movement of persons and EU citizenship
subtitle: Article 45 TFEU, the meaning of 'worker', and citizenship as its own source of rights
objectives: State the scope of Article 45 TFEU and the autonomous EU-law meaning of 'worker'
Explain how derived rights of residence attach to family members and how Union citizenship became a source of rights independent of economic activity
Apply the worker/public-policy/citizenship framework to new fact patterns, while correctly identifying that these rights no longer apply to UK nationals as a matter of current law

leadingAuthorities.role: The core provision guaranteeing free movement of workers within the Union

leadingAuthorities.citation: Van Duyn v Home Office [1974] ECR 1337
leadingAuthorities.role: Direct effect of the public-policy derogation; personal conduct required, not mere association

leadingAuthorities.citation: Union Royale Belge des Sociétés de Football Association v Bosman [1995] ECR I-4921
leadingAuthorities.role: Transfer fees and nationality quotas as restrictions on free movement of worker-athletes

leadingAuthorities.citation: Baumbast and R v SSHD [2002] ECR I-7091
leadingAuthorities.role: Union citizenship as a directly effective, freestanding source of residence rights

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: This is the module most students assume is 'dead law' because the UK has left. It isn't dead — it's the intellectual scaffolding behind most of the UK's own post-Brexit immigration and mobility rules, and examiners still test the doctrine on its own terms, historically. Learn it as you would learn any settled body of case law: precisely, and without assuming current entitlement.

profileHooks.weakApplication: You know the names — Bosman, Baumbast — but the exam question will hide the doctrine inside a fact pattern about a person crossing a border. Focus on the application items in this pool.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Parts 1 and 2 and nail down exactly what Article 45 protects and who counts as a 'worker' before moving on — the later parts assume you have that foundation solid.

overview.hook: In December 1995, a mid-table Belgian footballer named Jean-Marc Bosman changed the economics of professional sport forever — not by winning anything, but by refusing to accept that his own club could block a move to a French second-division side unless that club paid a transfer fee neither side wanted to pay. Bosman had nothing left: no club, no wages, effectively unemployable under a system that treated a footballer's labour as something his employer could still control after his contract had expired. He sued. Four years later, the European Court of Justice agreed with him, and in doing so demolished the transfer-fee system for out-of-contract players and every nationality quota in European club football — not because it liked football, but because Bosman was a 'worker' under Article 45 TFEU, and the rules restricted his free movement as surely as a border guard would have.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 1 September 2026. Everything in this lesson describes EU law as it was interpreted by the Court of Justice before the UK's exit, and is taught for its doctrinal and historical importance, not as law currently conferring rights on UK nationals. Since the end of the transition period on 31 December 2020, UK nationals no longer enjoy Article 45 free-movement rights, subject only to rights genuinely acquired before that date and protected under the Withdrawal Agreement (see the Citizens' Rights provisions implemented by the European Union (Withdrawal Agreement) Act 2020). Movement between the UK and the EU is now governed by ordinary immigration law on each side and by the more limited mobility provisions of the UK–EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement. Nothing in this lesson should be read as describing a right any current UK national holds by virtue of EU law.

parts.heading: Article 45: what counts as a restriction, and who is protected
parts.voice: case-narrative — builds the doctrine directly out of the Bosman facts
body: Article 45 TFEU guarantees workers the right to move freely between member states to take up and pursue employment, free of discrimination on grounds of nationality in employment, pay and other conditions of work. On its face this looks like an anti-discrimination provision. Bosman is the case that showed it is much more than that.

The transfer system Bosman challenged wasn't discriminatory on nationality at all — a Belgian club charging a fee to release a Belgian player to a French club treated him no differently from how it would have treated any player. The nationality quotas were a separate, additional problem: they capped the number of 'foreign' EU players a club could field, which plainly did discriminate on nationality. The Court struck both down, but for related reasons: both rules restricted a worker's ability to actually exercise free movement, whether or not they discriminated on the face of it.

This is the key doctrinal move to hold onto: Article 45 catches not only discriminatory rules, but any national or (as here) private-body rule that constitutes an obstacle to free movement, even a nationality-neutral one, unless it can be justified by an overriding requirement in the general interest and is proportionate. A transfer fee payable after a contract had already ended served no legitimate purpose recognised by the Court — it simply deterred players from moving.

components.definition: Under Article 45, a measure need not discriminate on nationality to infringe free movement — it is enough that the measure impedes or discourages a worker from leaving their home state to work elsewhere in the Union, unless objectively justified and proportionate.

interaction.prompt: In Bosman, was the transfer-fee rule (as opposed to the separate nationality quota) discriminatory on grounds of nationality?
options: No — it applied to all out-of-contract players regardless of nationality, but was still struck down as an obstacle to free movement
Yes — it only applied to players moving to a club in another member state
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct. This is the point examiners come back to: Article 45 reaches non-discriminatory obstacles, not just discriminatory ones.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again — the transfer fee applied to any out-of-contract player leaving his club. It wasn't nationality-based; it was struck down because it still discouraged the exercise of free movement.

parts.heading: Defining 'worker': an EU-law concept, not a national one
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: Article 45 protects 'workers', and the Court of Justice held early and consistently that 'worker' is an autonomous concept of EU law — member states cannot narrow it by defining employment status restrictively under their own domestic law, because that would let states quietly opt out of free movement by redefining who counts.

The settled test asks whether a person performs services of some economic value, for and under the direction of another, in return for remuneration, for a genuine and effective period — excluding activity so marginal and ancillary that it is not real economic activity at all. Bosman himself was plainly a worker on this test: he performed services (playing football) for his club, under its direction, for wages.

Once 'worker' status is established, Article 45 protects far more than the right to take the job itself. It protects equal treatment in pay and conditions, access to social and tax advantages on the same terms as nationals, and — critically for the next part of this lesson — derived rights of residence for the worker's family members, even where those family members are not themselves EU nationals.

components.label: The 'worker' test and what follows from it
points: Genuine and effective economic activity — not marginal or ancillary
Performed for and under the direction of another (subordination)
Nationality of the employer or sector is irrelevant — the test is functional, not formal
Once established: equal treatment in pay/conditions, access to social advantages, and derived residence rights for family members

interaction.prompt: Which of these best captures why the Court insists 'worker' is an autonomous EU-law concept rather than one defined by each member state?
options: Because otherwise a state could hollow out Article 45 simply by defining 'employee' narrowly under its own labour law
Because the Treaty itself contains a detailed statutory definition that leaves states no discretion at all
Because only self-employed persons were ever intended to be covered
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right — a uniform, EU-wide meaning is what stops the guarantee being defined away at national level.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The Treaty does not define 'worker' exhaustively; the Court supplied the functional test precisely so states couldn't narrow the category domestically.

parts.heading: The limits: public policy, and Van Duyn's refusal
parts.voice: Socratic — poses the dilemma before resolving it
body: If free movement of workers is this broad, what stops a state simply refusing entry to someone it dislikes? Article 45(3) itself carves out derogations for public policy, public security and public health — and Van Duyn v Home Office is the case that shows how narrowly the Court was prepared to let states use them.

Yvonne Van Duyn, a Dutch national, was refused leave to enter the UK to take up work with the Church of Scientology, which the UK government regarded (rightly or wrongly, as a matter of domestic policy) as socially undesirable, though not unlawful. The Home Office relied on the public-policy derogation.

The Court held two things that matter equally. First, the public-policy derogation in what is now Article 45(3) was itself directly effective — an individual could rely on it in a national court even without implementing legislation, an important building block for the whole doctrine of direct effect this module covers elsewhere. Second, and substantively, a state could take account of a person's association with a body considered socially harmful only if it also took genuine action against that body domestically, or otherwise treated the association as expressing objectionable personal conduct — mere membership of a lawful organisation, without more, was not itself enough to justify exclusion under a properly circumscribed public-policy exception.

The doctrinal lesson survives Van Duyn's own facts (which look dated today): a derogation from free movement must be pinned to the individual's own conduct, narrowly construed, and cannot be used as a general licence for a state to exclude anyone it finds distasteful.

components.factsShort: A Dutch national was refused UK entry to work for the Church of Scientology; the UK invoked the public-policy derogation.
components.ratioShort: The public-policy derogation is directly effective, but may only be invoked on the basis of the individual's own personal conduct — mere association with a lawful body is not, by itself, sufficient.

expanded.facts: Van Duyn intended to take up employment as a secretary with the Church of Scientology in the UK. The UK government considered Scientology socially harmful, although its activities were not unlawful, and refused her leave to enter on public-policy grounds under what was then Article 48(3) EEC.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Court held that member states retain a margin of discretion in assessing what public policy requires, but that discretion is not unlimited: the concept of personal conduct requires the derogation to be assessed against the individual, not merely by reference to the general undesirability of a group the state has not itself acted against.
expanded.significance: Van Duyn is doubly important: it is a leading direct-effect case (the public-policy derogation could be relied on directly in national proceedings) and a leading free-movement case establishing that derogations from Article 45 are construed narrowly and personally.

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that the Court treated as most significant in assessing whether the public-policy derogation was properly invoked.
interaction.scenarioText: Van Duyn wished to work for a legally operating organisation the UK government considered socially undesirable. The UK had not banned or taken enforcement action against that organisation domestically, but refused her entry on the basis that mere association with it was undesirable.
tappableSpans: had not banned or taken enforcement action
interaction.correctSpan: had not banned or taken enforcement action
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Exactly right. The absence of genuine domestic action against the body is what undermined the UK's reliance on personal conduct — the state can't treat association as disqualifying while tolerating the body itself.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the fact about consistency: what did the UK do, or not do, about the organisation itself, separately from Van Duyn? That's what the personal-conduct test turns on.

parts.heading: Beyond the market: citizenship as its own source of rights
parts.voice: argumentative — states the doctrinal shift and its significance
body: Everything so far has depended on economic activity: you had to be a worker, or a service-provider, to claim these rights. Baumbast and R v Secretary of State for the Home Department is the case that broke that link.

Mr Baumbast was a German national who had at one point worked in the UK but was no longer economically active there, and did not have comprehensive sickness insurance covering every requirement of the relevant residence directive. The second applicant, R, was a US national, divorced from an EU worker, caring for their children who remained in UK education. Neither fitted neatly inside the 'worker' framework built in Parts 1–3.

The Court held that Article 21 TFEU (then Article 18 EC) — the provision granting every citizen of the Union the right to move and reside freely within the territory of the member states — is directly effective and confers a free-standing right of residence, not merely a right parasitic on economic activity, subject only to the limitations and conditions laid down in the Treaty and secondary legislation, which must themselves be applied proportionately. For the children still in education, the Court also recognised a derived right for the parent-carer, drawing on earlier case law about children's right to continue schooling in the host state regardless of the parents' own residence status.

This is the conceptual pivot of the whole 'free movement of persons' story: from 1957 to the early 1990s, rights of movement were an incident of the internal market — you moved because you worked, and the rights followed the economic activity. Baumbast confirms that Union citizenship itself, introduced by the Maastricht Treaty, had by the early 2000s become an independent legal status capable of generating rights the Treaty's economic provisions never needed to supply.

components.title: From worker to citizen: how the source of the right changed
components.description: Tracks the doctrinal shift in what has to be shown to claim a right of residence.

nodes.label: Is the claimant a 'worker' under Article 45 (genuine, effective, subordinate, remunerated activity)?
Yes → Article 45 rights: equal treatment, residence, derived family rights
No → is the claimant self-sufficient / does Article 21 TFEU citizenship apply directly?
Yes → directly effective Article 21 right of residence, subject to proportionate conditions (Baumbast)
Special case: child of an EU worker in education in the host state → derived right for the primary carer, regardless of the carer's own status

components.textAlternative: First ask whether the claimant is a 'worker' under Article 45 — if so, the full package of worker rights applies, including derived family rights. If not, ask whether Article 21 TFEU citizenship rights apply directly and independently of economic activity, as in Baumbast, subject to proportionate conditions. A further derived route exists for a parent caring for a worker's child still in education in the host state, regardless of the parent's own economic or immigration status.

interaction.prompt: Which scenario most directly mirrors the reasoning in Baumbast, rather than the worker-based reasoning of Bosman?
interaction.scenarioA: A German national moves to France, takes up a full-time salaried job there, and claims equal access to a housing benefit available to French nationals.
interaction.scenarioB: A retired German national, no longer economically active and relying on private means rather than fully comprehensive sickness insurance, claims a right to continue residing in the UK under EU citizenship provisions.
interaction.explanation: B mirrors Baumbast precisely: a claimant who cannot rely on worker status invokes Article 21 citizenship as a free-standing source of a residence right, subject to proportionality. A is a straightforward worker-equal-treatment claim under Article 45, the Bosman-style route.

parts.heading: Then and now: why UK nationals no longer hold these rights
parts.voice: direct — closes the doctrinal arc with the current legal reality
body: Everything in this lesson describes a body of law that shaped decades of UK legal practice, immigration policy and academic doctrine — and that, as a matter of current entitlement, UK nationals no longer benefit from. That is not a footnote; it is the single most important thing to get right in an exam answer that touches this module.

The UK's withdrawal ended the direct application of Article 45 and Article 21 TFEU to UK nationals at the close of the transition period, 31 December 2020. The Withdrawal Agreement preserves rights genuinely acquired by that date — a UK national already lawfully resident and economically active in, say, Spain before the deadline generally keeps a protected status there, and the reverse is true for EU nationals already resident in the UK, now administered through the EU Settlement Scheme. But nobody exercising 'free movement' for the first time today, on either side, is doing so under Article 45 or Article 21.

In their place sit two separate frameworks: each state's own immigration law (for the UK, the points-based system now applied to EU nationals exactly as to any other third-country national), and the narrower mobility provisions of the UK–EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement, which permit limited business-visitor and short-term movement but nothing close to the Baumbast-level free-standing residence right. An exam script that treats a present-day UK national as still holding Article 45 rights is making a basic factual error, however well it explains the underlying doctrine.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students who know the doctrine well sometimes write answers as if a UK national today could simply invoke Article 45 or Baumbast-style citizenship rights to work or reside in an EU member state.
components.whyItsWrong: Those rights ended for UK nationals at the end of the transition period (31 December 2020), except where already acquired and protected under the Withdrawal Agreement. Current mobility for UK nationals is governed by each state's own immigration law and by the TCA's much narrower provisions — not by TFEU free movement.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that a UK national moving to an EU member state for the first time today can rely directly on Article 45 TFEU?
interaction.explanation: Cannot. Article 45 stopped applying to UK nationals at the end of the transition period. Only rights genuinely acquired before 31 December 2020 are protected, under the Withdrawal Agreement — first-time movement today is governed by ordinary immigration law and the TCA, not by EU free movement.

testPool.prompt: Which Treaty article guarantees free movement of workers within the EU?
testPool.modelAnswer: Article 45 TFEU guarantees the free movement of workers, prohibiting discrimination on grounds of nationality as regards employment, remuneration and other conditions of work and employment.

testPool.prompt: Is 'worker' under Article 45 defined by each member state's own domestic employment law?
options: No — it is an autonomous EU-law concept applied uniformly across member states
Yes — each state may define who counts as a worker for the purposes of Article 45

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the elements of the Court's functional test for 'worker' status?
options: Genuine and effective economic activity
Performance of services under the direction of another
Remuneration
Possession of a written contract of employment lasting at least one year
testPool.trapExplanation: There is no minimum contract length or requirement of a written contract in the Court's test. Students sometimes import UK domestic employment-law concepts (like a minimum qualifying period) that have no place in the EU-law 'worker' test.

testPool.prompt: Order the reasoning steps the Court of Justice followed in Bosman to hold the transfer-fee rule unlawful.
items: Establish that Bosman was a 'worker' performing genuine economic activity
Ask whether the transfer-fee rule constituted an obstacle to free movement, discriminatory or not
Consider whether the rule could be justified by an overriding requirement in the general interest
Hold the rule disproportionate and therefore contrary to Article 45

testPool.prompt: Article 45(3) permits member states to restrict free movement on grounds of public policy, public security and public health. What did Van Duyn add to the interpretation of that derogation?
options: That the derogation is directly effective and must be assessed on the basis of the individual's own personal conduct, not mere association with a group
That the derogation cannot be relied upon by any member state under any circumstances
That the derogation only applies to criminal convictions

testPool.prompt: In the passage below adapted from Baumbast, highlight the sentence stating the ratio on citizenship rights.
testPool.passage: The applicant no longer satisfied the strict conditions of the relevant residence directive because his sickness insurance did not cover every contingency in the host state. Nonetheless, citizens of the Union are entitled to rely directly on Article 21 TFEU, which confers a free-standing right of residence subject only to the limitations and conditions laid down in the Treaties and secondary legislation, applied in a manner consistent with the principle of proportionality. A refusal of residence on a narrow, disproportionate application of those conditions is therefore unlawful.
testPool.ratioSentence: Nonetheless, citizens of the Union are entitled to rely directly on Article 21 TFEU, which confers a free-standing right of residence subject only to the limitations and conditions laid down in the Treaties and secondary legislation, applied in a manner consistent with the principle of proportionality.

testPool.prompt: An Italian professional cyclist, contracted to a Belgian team, is barred by a cycling federation rule from racing for any team in another member state unless that new team pays a fee to his current team, even though his contract has expired. Applying Bosman, is this rule likely to infringe Article 45?
options: Yes — an out-of-contract transfer fee restricting a worker's movement between clubs in different member states is the precise type of obstacle Bosman condemned
No — sport is entirely outside the scope of EU law
No — because the rule applies to Italian and Belgian clubs equally, it cannot infringe Article 45
testPool.explanation: This is materially identical to Bosman's own facts: an out-of-contract fee deterring movement between clubs in different member states. Equal application to all nationalities does not save a rule that still obstructs free movement — Article 45 catches non-discriminatory obstacles too.

testPool.prompt: A French national works part-time (six hours a week) stacking shelves in Germany purely to supplement a student loan, earning a small wage. Is she likely to satisfy the 'worker' test?
options: Possibly not — if the activity is so marginal and ancillary as not to constitute genuine and effective economic activity, though a small amount of paid, subordinate work can still qualify; the facts would need closer examination
Yes automatically — any paid work of any kind and duration always qualifies without further inquiry
No — only full-time employment can ever satisfy the worker test
testPool.explanation: The test asks about genuineness and effectiveness, not a fixed number of hours; marginal, purely ancillary activity may fall short, but modest part-time paid work performed under direction is not automatically excluded either — this is a classic borderline application question.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that would most strengthen a claim to a free-standing Article 21 citizenship right of residence, on Baumbast reasoning, for someone who is not a 'worker'.
testPool.scenarioText: A Polish national retired early and moved to Portugal. She is not employed, but has adequate private means to support herself and holds private medical insurance that does not meet every technical requirement of the relevant secondary legislation.
tappableSpans: does not meet every technical requirement
testPool.explanation: Self-sufficiency (adequate resources, even if the insurance technically falls short) is what allows a Baumbast-style argument that a disproportionately strict application of the secondary-legislation conditions should not defeat the directly effective Article 21 right.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario is closer to Van Duyn's reasoning than to Baumbast's?
testPool.scenarioA: A member state refuses entry to a national of another member state solely because of her lawful membership of a political party the state dislikes, without having taken any domestic action against that party.
testPool.scenarioB: A member state refuses a residence card to an economically inactive citizen of another member state who has adequate resources but imperfect insurance cover.
testPool.explanation: A raises the Van Duyn public-policy/personal-conduct question directly. B is a Baumbast-style citizenship/proportionality question about the conditions attached to Article 21 residence, not a public-policy derogation case.

testPool.prompt: A UK national wants to move to Germany today to take up employment there for the first time, with no prior residence history in Germany before 2021. Can she rely on Article 45 TFEU?
options: No — Article 45 no longer applies to UK nationals; her position is governed by German immigration law and any relevant UK–EU agreement
Yes — Article 45 continues to apply to UK nationals exactly as before

testPool.prompt: A Spanish national, Elena, took up salaried employment in the UK in 2018 and has lived there continuously since, now protected under the Withdrawal Agreement. Her adult son, a Spanish national with no independent means, wishes to join her in the UK for the first time in 2026. Analyse, using the doctrine in this lesson plus the framing on post-Brexit rights, whether the son can rely on EU free-movement law to join her.
factsToOrder: Elena took up employment in the UK in 2018, before the end of the transition period
Elena is now protected under the Withdrawal Agreement in respect of rights acquired by 31 December 2020
The son seeks to join her for the first time in 2026
The son has no independent means and would be relying on a derived right
The claimed derived right would need to arise now, in 2026, not before the transition period ended

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the son can rely on EU free-movement law (worker-derived family rights or Article 21 citizenship) to join Elena in the UK for the first time in 2026.
modelAnswer.rule: Derived family rights and Article 21 citizenship rights under EU law no longer apply to new claims involving the UK; the Withdrawal Agreement protects only rights genuinely acquired, exercised or existing by the end of the transition period on 31 December 2020. A wholly new family-reunification claim arising in 2026 falls outside that protection.
modelAnswer.application: Elena's own residence is protected because it was acquired before the deadline. But the son's claim to join her is new and arises only in 2026 — it was not an existing right as at 31 December 2020, and EU free-movement doctrine (worker-derived rights, Baumbast-style citizenship reasoning) no longer generates rights for UK-related movement of this kind.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The son cannot rely on EU free-movement law; his position must instead be assessed under ordinary UK immigration rules for family reunification, not under Article 45 or Article 21 TFEU.

testPool.prompt: Which statement best explains why Baumbast marks a doctrinal shift from the worker-based cases like Bosman?
options: Because Baumbast held that citizenship confers rights independent of economic activity, whereas Bosman's reasoning depended entirely on the claimant's status as an economically active worker
Because Baumbast overruled Bosman
Because Baumbast concerned goods rather than persons
testPool.trapExplanation: Baumbast does not overrule Bosman — the two operate on different legal bases (citizenship vs worker status) that coexist. The shift is additive, not a reversal, and neither case concerns goods.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that a UK national who was already lawfully resident and working in France before 31 December 2020 has lost all protection of that residence today?
testPool.explanation: Rights genuinely acquired before the end of the transition period are protected under the Withdrawal Agreement, administered in each state's own residence-status scheme — this is the important exception to the general loss of Article 45/21 rights for UK nationals.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is doctrinal drift into the present tense — writing as if Article 45 or Article 21 still confer rights on UK nationals today. Get the historical doctrine right, then get the current legal position right separately; conflating them is the single biggest way to lose marks in this module.
